question: In experiments with large language models, which method had the best performance?
answer:
The best performance in the large language model (LLM) experiments was achieved by combining **few-shot prompting with chain-of-thought prompting**, yielding an F1-score of 0.558.

Additionally, a report using role-based, few-shot, and chain-of-thought prompting also reached this best generative AI performance level (F1-score = 0.558).

sources.quote: We also fine-tuned the Llama-3-8B [25] large language model (LLM), using 10 epochs and a learning rate of 5e-5.

To address the class imbalance, we performed an additional experiment with the BERT-based classifier in which we under-sampled the "negative" (i.e., majority) class in the training set by removing sentences that were not similar to any of the sentences in the "positive" (i.e., the minority) class.
Our bestperforming generative AI approach, however, was outperformed by all of our machine learning-based classifiers that used manually annotated training.

While the best performance of our generative AI approach was achieved using role-based, few-shot, and chain-of-thought prompting (F1-score = 0.558), it was nonetheless outperformed by all of our machine learning-based classifiers.

It marginally outperformed classifiers based on BiomedBERT-Base-Abstract-Fulltext (0.767)—a smaller model pre-trained on PubMed abstracts and PubMed Central full-text articles—and COVID-Twitter-BERT (0.766)—a model pre-trained on Twitter posts related to COVID-19.
